To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

we find a strong radial (galaxy centerward) alignment effect for satellite galaxies in close proximity (<300 kpc) to a central host galaxy, but that this alignment effect is not seen for satellite galaxies at larger distances.

the orientation of satellite galaxies is correlated with the orientation of their host galaxies, that the correlation is stronger for more massive hosts and for closer satellites, and that the strength of the correlation depends on the method used for estimating galaxy orientation.

we have identified and quantified alignment effects among host-satellite galaxy pairs, and that these alignment effects are dependent on the method used for measuring the orientation of the satellite galaxies.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the study of galaxy interactions, mergers and their effects on the properties of the galaxies involved.
the study of the alignment between galaxies in a large sample of the Sloan Digital Sky Survey.
the alignment of galaxies and the effects of galaxy interactions on the morphology, dynamics, and orientation of galaxies.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
galaxy orientation and alignment effects are real, but are difficult to characterize in a meaningful way.
galaxy alignment effects are real but are not well understood.

there is a strong radial alignment signal for highly concentrated satellite galaxies at small projected separation from their hosts, but that this signal is significantly weaker when using galaxy model orientations.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the Holmberg effect is real, but it is a very small effect and is difficult to detect.
we find evidence for alignment between the host galaxies and the satellites.
the Holmberg Effect is real, but is not as strong as previously thought, and that the alignment of nearby galaxies with their HGs is not as strong a phenomenon as previously thought.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the nature of alignment effects among galaxy populations depends on the selection criteria and the method used to measure galaxy orientation.
the nature of the alignment effect is highly sensitive to the selection of the host galaxy and the method of measuring galaxy orientations.

, in order to make progress on understanding the nature and origins of these effects, a more uniform and complete galaxy catalog, and a larger sample of galaxies with well-determined orientation, are needed.
